**Output Diversity and Mode Collapse in Language Models.** The tendency of language models to produce repetitive, low-diversity outputs has been recognized since early studies of neural text degeneration. Holtzman et al. [1] identified that maximization-based decoding strategies such as beam search cause language models to sample from the unreliable tail of the probability distribution, leading to bland and repetitive text, and proposed nucleus sampling as a remedy. Subsequent work has systematically characterized diversity collapse in the context of post-training and alignment. Mohammadi [2] showed that RLHF-aligned models exhibit lower token-level entropy, clustered embedding representations, and convergence toward attractor states, demonstrating that alignment reduces both syntactic and semantic diversity in creative generation tasks. Guo et al. [3] introduced a comprehensive framework for benchmarking linguistic diversity along lexical, syntactic, and semantic dimensions, finding that state-of-the-art LLMs systematically underrepresent creative linguistic structures compared to human text. Yun et al. [4] identified diversity collapse induced by structured prompt templates, showing that role markers and special tokens act as behavioral anchors that suppress output variation even under high-temperature sampling. Beyond diagnosing the problem, several works have proposed mitigation strategies. Nguyen et al. [6] introduced min-p sampling, a dynamic decoding strategy that adjusts the truncation threshold based on the top token's probability, improving both coherence and diversity at high temperatures. Most closely related to the target paper, Zhang et al. [5] proposed NoveltyBench, a benchmark for evaluating the ability of language models to generate multiple distinct and high-quality outputs. NoveltyBench uses curated prompts and filtered real-world queries and finds that larger models within a family often exhibit less diversity than smaller ones. However, existing diversity evaluations have largely focused on intra-model repetition, with limited attention to inter-model homogeneity, and have not provided a comprehensive taxonomy of the types of open-ended queries that users pose to language models in practice. This motivates the target paper's introduction of a large-scale dataset with a fine-grained taxonomy of real-world open-ended queries, as well as a systematic analysis of both intra-model repetition and cross-model output convergence.

**Real-World Conversation Datasets and Open-Ended Query Resources.** Large-scale datasets of real-world user interactions with language models have emerged as critical resources for studying LLM behavior in naturalistic settings. Zhao et al. [7] introduced WildChat, a corpus of one million user-ChatGPT conversations collected through an opt-in public chat service, encompassing over 2.5 million interaction turns with demographic metadata. WildChat has been shown to offer greater linguistic diversity and more varied use cases than prior instruction-tuning datasets. Zheng et al. [8] released LMSYS-Chat-1M, a dataset of one million real-world conversations with 25 different LLMs collected from the Vicuna demo and Chatbot Arena, demonstrating its utility for content moderation, safety benchmarking, and instruction-following training. These datasets provide valuable resources for understanding how users interact with LLMs at scale. However, they are primarily designed to capture broad interaction patterns rather than to systematically characterize open-ended queries that admit multiple valid responses. Neither dataset provides a systematic taxonomy of query types or distinguishes open-ended from closed-ended prompts. The target paper addresses this gap by filtering and categorizing open-ended user queries from WildChat, constructing the first comprehensive taxonomy of open-ended query types, and coupling this taxonomy with dense human annotations to enable the study of both generative diversity and pluralistic preference alignment.

**Pluralistic Alignment, Reward Modeling, and Human Preference Diversity.** Standard alignment pipelines typically assume a single, consensus notion of quality and train models to optimize for majority preferences. A growing body of work has challenged this assumption by examining annotator disagreement and modeling diverse human preferences. Davani et al. [9] showed that treating annotator judgments as separate subtasks rather than aggregating to a single ground truth preserves systematic individual differences and produces better-calibrated uncertainty estimates in subjective NLP tasks. Bakker et al. [10] fine-tuned a 70B-parameter LLM to generate consensus statements that maximize expected approval across groups with diverse opinions, demonstrating that language models can synthesize outputs reflecting heterogeneous preferences when trained with appropriate social welfare objectives. Castricato et al. [11] introduced PERSONA, a reproducible testbed for pluralistic alignment that procedurally generates diverse user profiles from demographic data and evaluates whether LMs can role-play users with varied values. Zhang et al. [12] developed a taxonomy of disagreement sources in human preference annotations, showing that over 30% of disagreements stem from genuine preference diversity rather than annotation error, and demonstrated that standard Bradley-Terry reward models fail to distinguish between consensus and contested preferences. Complementing these empirical findings, Xie et al. [13] provided a survey of personalized and pluralistic preference alignment techniques, categorizing methods into training-time, inference-time, and user-modeling approaches, and highlighting the lack of standardized benchmarks for evaluating personalization. In parallel, the evaluation of reward models themselves has been systematized through benchmarks such as RewardBench [14], which evaluates over 80 reward models across chat, reasoning, and safety domains, revealing systematic shortcomings in reasoning and generalization. However, existing work on pluralistic alignment has largely studied preference diversity through synthetic personas or aggregated crowd preferences, rather than through dense, per-example human annotations that capture the full distribution of individual annotator judgments on alternative responses to open-ended queries. The target paper contributes a large-scale dataset with 25 independent human annotations per example, enabling fine-grained analysis of when and how human preferences diverge, and systematically evaluates whether LMs, reward models, and LM judges remain calibrated to human ratings under conditions of high annotator disagreement and similar-quality alternative responses.

tldr.text: [research paper] Neural text degeneration arises because language models' probability distributions have an unreliable tail of low-probability tokens that dominate under maximization-based decoding (e.g., beam search), leading to repetitive, incoherent outputs. Nucleus Sampling mitigates this by dynamically truncating the tail and sampling from the top-p probability mass, preserving both high-quality, diverse text and human-like variability—outperforming beam search, top-k sampling, and pure sampling in human and statistical evaluations.

The study demonstrates that LLMs systematically underrepresent creative linguistic structures—particularly in story generation—due to training data homogenization and conservative decoding strategies, and shows that diversity is strongly influenced by model scale, training data, decoding methods, and fine-tuning stages, with syntactic diversity being most vulnerable to degradation during pretraining and preference tuning.

s2_metadata.title: The Price of Format: Diversity Collapse in LLMs

tldr.text: [empirical research paper] The paper identifies 'diversity collapse' in instruction-tuned LLMs, where structured prompt templates—such as role markers and special tokens—induce semantically similar outputs in open-ended generation, even under high-temperature sampling. Through controlled ablations, it shows that structural tokens act as behavioral anchors, suppressing early-stage entropy and limiting topical and semantic diversity, with fully open-ended prompts achieving the highest variation. The effect is task-dependent: formatting is critical for structure-sensitive tasks (e.g., GSM8K, IFEval) but harms performance on knowledge-intensive tasks (e.g., MMLU), revealing a trade-off between alignment consistency and output diversity.

s2_metadata.title: NoveltyBench: Evaluating Language Models for Humanlike Diversity

tldr.text: [research paper] NoveltyBench introduces a benchmark to evaluate language models' ability to generate diverse, high-quality outputs by assessing response variation across subjectivity, randomness, creativity, and factual knowledge. It reveals that state-of-the-art models exhibit significant mode collapse, with larger models in the same family producing less diversity than smaller ones, challenging the assumption that model scale correlates with generative diversity. The benchmark uses human-annotated ground truth and introduces a unified novelty-quality metric that measures distinct equivalence classes and user patience-weighted utility, exposing a critical gap in current training and evaluation paradigms.

tldr.text: [research paper] PERSONA introduces a scalable, reproducible testbed for evaluating pluralistic alignment in language models using 1,586 synthetic personas derived from US census data. These personas are procedurally constructed with realistic demographic and idiosyncratic attributes, enabling large-scale generation of 317,200 feedback pairs across 3,868 prompts on value-laden topics. The framework enables systematic evaluation of LMs in role-playing diverse users, validates alignment capabilities via human judgment, and establishes a benchmark dataset (PERSONA Bench) for future research in pluralistic and personalized alignment.

tldr.text: [research paper] The paper reveals that over 30% of human preference annotations in LLM datasets stem from diverging individual predilections—such as response style, verbosity, or interpretive differences—rather than annotation errors. Standard reward modeling methods (e.g., Bradley-Terry) fail to distinguish between high-agreement and divergent preferences, leading to biased training where models learn a single dominant response. The authors propose modeling preferences as distributions over user judgments and introduce methods to detect divergent preferences in LLM-as-Judge evaluations, enabling more pluralistically aligned systems that respect user diversity in judgment.

s2_metadata.title: A Survey on Personalized and Pluralistic Preference Alignment in Large Language Models

tldr.text: This survey introduces a taxonomy of personalized and pluralistic preference alignment in large language models (LLMs), distinguishing between training-time and inference-time methods that adapt LLM behavior to individual, contextual, and group-specific user preferences. It highlights that dynamic user preferences—such as tone, style, and response context—require methods like logit rectification, preference-based re-alignment, and user modeling, while emphasizing the lack of standardized benchmarks and open challenges in evaluating personalization effectiveness across diverse user scenarios.

\section{Related Work}
The diversity collapse problem of LMs. Diversity collapse, characterized by the inability of LMs to generate diverse outputs, presents a significant challenge to pluralistic alignment research [96, 78, 23, 93, 53, 91]. Prior studies identify some key factors contributing to diversity collapse, including training on synthetic data [33, 86, 93, 79], LM alignment [58, 41, 43], and insufficient diversity in training data [15]. Potential consequences of diversity collapse include reduced creativity, loss of minority perspectives, spread of bias, and overall decline in model utility and trustworthiness [5, 38, 21]. In response, a range of mitigation strategies are proposed, such as training corpora diversification [87, 68, 88, 34], training algorithm modifications [95, 54], alternative decoding [85, 62] and prompting [94, 11] strategies.

Measuring the creativity and divergent thinking of language models. Recent efforts to measure the creativity and divergent thinking of LMs often adapt established psychometric tests. For example, [16] utilizes a divergent association task (DAT) by asking models to generate semantically distant or unrelated words [63]. Similarly, tasks such as the Alternate Uses Test (AUT) [69], the Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking (TTCT) [1, 13], Human Evaluation, and LLM-as-a-judge [46] are employed to assess dimensions like fluency, originality, complexity, and effective semantic diversity [80] of LM responses. Despite these demonstrated capabilities, LLM-generated creative content tends towards homogeneity, even when individual outputs achieve high creativity scores [90]. To address these evaluation complexities, some benchmarks, such as [72, 56, 66, 95], focus on specific creative abilities like scientific idea and code generation. Other works propose new metrics [61]. While LMs show promise in creative tasks, comprehensively evaluating their creativity remains an active and challenging research area [44]. We conduct a large-scale systematic study of real-world open-ended user queries and provide a comprehensive taxonomy, query dataset, and dense human annotations to improve evaluation and model training for reducing mode collapse in language models.

Disagreement and pluralistic alignment of language models. Advances in AI value alignment research have substantially improved LM utility and safety, through enhanced training processes [75, 64, 70], and the use of both synthetic data [30] and human datasets [8, 29]. Yet, a significant challenge remains: the potential for monolithic value representation [73, 74]. In contrast, the emerging focus on pluralistic alignment emphasizes the need for AI to serve the varied demands of a wide population [81, 2]. This shift is driving innovation in methods [19, 62, 49, 14, 26, 83], benchmarks [12], and data collection strategies [42, 76] to support this vision of diversity. Additionally, approaches leveraging multiple LMs interacting through system messages are also being explored to boost variety [84, 17, 59]. Parallel efforts are dedicated to quantifying and improving the cultural diversity exhibited by LLMs [71, 77, 18, 60, 52]. Yet, a common characteristic of many existing pluralistic alignment work is its reliance on predefined diversity dimensions, like demographics [48, 57], personality style [51, 35, 98, 65], and cultural background [92, 22, 4]. To enable models that genuinely cater to individuality without relying on stereotypes, individual-level alignment is needed [36, 98].

tldr.text: [research paper] The paper presents a comprehensive study of reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) for training language models to be helpful and harmless. It introduces an iterated online RLHF training process where preference models and policies are updated weekly with fresh human feedback, leading to sustained improvements in both helpfulness and harmlessness. A key finding is a roughly linear relationship between the RL reward and the square root of the KL divergence between policy and initialization, indicating a predictable trade-off in policy divergence. The results show that RLHF does not degrade performance on most NLP tasks—especially for larger models—and can be effectively combined with specialized skill training (e.g., code generation) without compromising alignment or capability.

topics.label: Diversity Collapse Problem of LMs
topics.summary: Diversity collapse, the inability of LMs to generate diverse outputs, challenges pluralistic alignment. Key factors include training on synthetic data, LM alignment, and insufficient data diversity. Consequences include reduced creativity, minority perspective loss, bias, and lower utility. Mitigations involve training corpora diversification, algorithm modifications, alternative decoding, and prompting.

topics.label: Measuring Creativity and Divergent Thinking of LMs
topics.summary: Recent efforts adapt psychometric tests like DAT, AUT, TTCT, human evaluation, and LLM-as-a-judge. Despite high individual creativity scores, content tends toward homogeneity. Benchmarks focus on specific abilities like scientific idea generation, and new metrics are proposed. Comprehensive evaluation remains challenging. The current work studies real-world open-ended queries to reduce mode collapse.

topics.label: Disagreement and Pluralistic Alignment of LMs
topics.summary: Advances in alignment improve utility and safety but risk monolithic value representation. Pluralistic alignment aims to serve diverse populations, driving innovations in methods, benchmarks, and data collection. Approaches include multi-LM interactions and cultural diversity quantification. Current work often relies on predefined diversity dimensions; individual-level alignment is needed to avoid stereotypes.

claims.text: Holtzman et al. identified that maximization-based decoding (e.g., beam search) leads to bland and repetitive text and proposed nucleus sampling.
Mohammadi showed that RLHF-aligned models exhibit lower token-level entropy, clustered embedding representations, and convergence toward attractor states, reducing diversity.
Guo et al. introduced a framework for benchmarking linguistic diversity along lexical, syntactic, and semantic dimensions, finding that LLMs underrepresent creative structures.
Yun et al. identified diversity collapse induced by structured prompt templates and role markers.
Nguyen et al. introduced min-p sampling, which adjusts truncation threshold based on top token probability to improve coherence and diversity.
Zhang et al. proposed NoveltyBench, a benchmark for evaluating multiple distinct outputs, and found that larger models often exhibit less diversity.
Existing diversity evaluations focus on intra-model repetition with limited attention to inter-model homogeneity and lack a comprehensive taxonomy of open-ended queries.
The target paper introduces a large-scale dataset with a fine-grained taxonomy of open-ended queries and systematic analysis of intra- and cross-model diversity.
Zhao et al. introduced WildChat, a corpus of one million user-ChatGPT conversations with over 2.5 million interaction turns and demographic metadata.
Zheng et al. released LMSYS-Chat-1M, a dataset of one million real-world conversations with 25 different LLMs.
Neither WildChat nor LMSYS-Chat-1M provides a systematic taxonomy of query types or distinguishes open-ended from closed-ended prompts.
The target paper addresses this gap by filtering and categorizing open-ended queries from WildChat and constructing a comprehensive taxonomy.
Davani et al. showed that treating annotator judgments as separate subtasks preserves individual differences and produces better-calibrated uncertainty estimates.
Bakker et al. fine-tuned a 70B-parameter LLM to generate consensus statements maximizing expected approval across groups with diverse opinions.
Castricato et al. introduced PERSONA, a testbed for pluralistic alignment that uses procedurally generated user profiles.
Zhang et al. developed a taxonomy of disagreement sources in human preference annotations, showing over 30% of disagreements are from genuine preference diversity.
Standard Bradley-Terry reward models fail to distinguish between consensus and contested preferences.
Xie et al. provided a survey of personalized and pluralistic preference alignment techniques.
RewardBench evaluates over 80 reward models across chat, reasoning, and safety domains, revealing systematic shortcomings in reasoning and generalization.
Existing work on pluralistic alignment has largely studied preference diversity through synthetic personas or aggregated crowd preferences.
The target paper contributes a large-scale dataset with 25 independent human annotations per example and evaluates calibration under high annotator disagreement.
